meta.name: CompTIA Cloud+ (CV0-004)
meta.notes: initial pack — 12 questions across the five CV0-004 domains (architecture/design, deployment, operations, security, troubleshooting) [scheduled-agent]

questions.question: A cloud architect designs a customer-facing web tier that must survive the loss of an entire availability zone with no manual intervention. Which deployment pattern best meets this requirement?
options: Single VM with a daily snapshot copied to another zone
An auto-scaling group of instances spread across multiple availability zones behind a regional load balancer
An active/passive pair in the same availability zone with a floating IP
A single large VM with an attached replicated block volume
questions.explanation: Multi-AZ auto-scaling behind a regional load balancer is the canonical high-availability pattern: instances in another zone keep serving traffic if a zone fails, and new capacity is launched automatically. A single snapshot strategy still requires manual recovery and accepts data loss. Same-zone active/passive does not survive a zone outage. One large VM is a single point of failure even with replicated storage.

questions.question: A SaaS provider must minimise its Recovery Point Objective (RPO) for an OLTP database while keeping cost reasonable. Which replication approach best fits the requirement?
options: Nightly full backups shipped to object storage
Asynchronous replication to a warm secondary every four hours
Synchronous replication to a standby in another availability zone
Reliance on the underlying storage array's RAID 6 parity
questions.explanation: Synchronous replication commits each transaction on the primary and standby before acknowledging, giving an RPO at or near zero — the right answer when data loss must be minimised. Asynchronous replication leaves a measurable gap (here up to four hours). Nightly backups leave up to 24 hours of unprotected data. RAID 6 protects against disk failure but not against site, host, or logical failures, so it is not a replication strategy.

questions.question: An operations team wants every production environment built identically, fully versioned in Git, and reproducible in seconds for blue/green deployments. Which practice best supports this goal?
options: Manual click-through builds documented in a runbook
Imperative shell scripts SSH'd to each host after provisioning
Declarative Infrastructure as Code applied through a CI/CD pipeline
Golden images cloned by hand whenever a change is needed
questions.explanation: Declarative IaC (Terraform, Bicep, CloudFormation, etc.) describes the desired end state, is reviewable in pull requests, and can be applied automatically from a pipeline — making environments reproducible and auditable. Manual click-ops and hand-cloned images drift over time and are not versioned. Imperative SSH scripts can work once but are order-sensitive and harder to make idempotent than declarative IaC.

questions.question: A DevOps engineer must move a stateful application that bundles its database, message broker, and web tier into a Kubernetes cluster. Which approach correctly addresses the database tier?
options: Deploy the database as a standard Deployment and rely on the ReplicaSet for data persistence
Run the database in a StatefulSet with stable network identities and PersistentVolumeClaims
Run the database in a DaemonSet so one copy is scheduled on every node
Bake the database files into the container image so they ship with each pod
questions.explanation: StatefulSets provide each pod with a stable, ordinal hostname and a unique PersistentVolumeClaim, which is what databases and other stateful workloads need for safe restart, scaling, and replication. Deployments and ReplicaSets are designed for stateless pods; their replicas are interchangeable and storage is not stable. DaemonSets target node-level agents, not clustered databases. Baking data into images loses it on every redeploy and prevents recovery.

questions.question: An auditor asks how the cloud provider's responsibility for security boundaries differs across service models in the shared responsibility model. Which statement is correct?
options: In IaaS the customer is responsible for the hypervisor patching
In PaaS the customer manages the underlying OS and runtime patches
In SaaS the provider manages application, runtime, OS, and infrastructure, and the customer is mainly responsible for data, identities, and access configuration
In all three models the provider is responsible for the customer's data classification
questions.explanation: Under SaaS the provider runs the application stack end-to-end, and the customer's job centres on identity, access management, and the data they put in. In IaaS the hypervisor is the provider's responsibility — the customer patches the guest OS and above. In PaaS the provider also handles OS and runtime patching; the customer focuses on application code and data. Data classification is always the customer's responsibility regardless of service model.

questions.question: A security engineer wants developers to retrieve database credentials at runtime without ever storing them in code, container images, or environment variables checked into version control. Which solution best meets the requirement?
options: Embed an encrypted properties file in the image and decrypt at start-up with a shared passphrase
Pull short-lived secrets from a managed secrets manager (for example HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager) using a workload identity
Push credentials to each host with a configuration-management tool every time they rotate
Store credentials in a private Git repository protected by branch permissions
questions.explanation: A managed secrets manager combined with workload identity lets the running process authenticate as itself, fetch the credential at startup, and rely on automatic rotation — there is no static secret to leak. Encrypted files still hide a long-lived passphrase that has to live somewhere. Pushing credentials with config-management leaves them on disk and in logs. Storing credentials in Git, even privately, is the anti-pattern this question is testing.

questions.question: An ops engineer is reviewing a web tier whose CPU is spiking to 100 percent every weekday at 09:00, causing slow page loads. Which scaling configuration is the most appropriate first response?
options: Vertical scaling — manually resize the instances to a larger size every Monday morning
Predictive or scheduled scaling — pre-warm capacity ahead of the known 09:00 traffic surge
Disable health checks so unhealthy instances continue serving traffic
Increase the cool-down period so the auto-scaling group reacts less often
questions.explanation: Because the spike happens at a known, repeatable time, scheduled (or predictive) scaling pre-warms capacity before the surge and removes the lag of reactive scaling. Vertical scaling does not address the spiky pattern and forces a restart. Disabling health checks compromises reliability and hides problems. Increasing the cool-down makes scaling slower, which is the opposite of what is needed.

questions.question: Users report that an internal application is unreachable from one virtual network but reachable from another. Routing tables and security groups look correct, but the destination is in a peered VPC. Which check most often resolves this class of issue?
options: Confirm that transitive peering is configured — peering is non-transitive by default, so a third VPC needs its own peering or a transit gateway
Re-issue the TLS certificate on the destination service
Increase the MTU on the source instances to 9001
Disable source/destination check on the destination NIC
questions.explanation: VPC peering is non-transitive: VPC A peered with B and B peered with C does not give A a path to C. Either add direct peering A↔C or use a transit gateway / hub-and-spoke construct. TLS certificates do not control reachability. Jumbo frames are a throughput tweak, not a reachability fix. Disabling source/destination check is only relevant when a NIC forwards traffic, such as on a NAT appliance.

questions.question: A FinOps lead wants to cut steady-state compute spend on workloads that run 24x7 for at least one year, without changing the architecture. Which purchasing option is the best fit?
options: Spot or preemptible instances
On-demand instances paid per second
Reserved instances or 1-year savings-plan commitments
Dedicated hosts billed per physical socket
questions.explanation: For predictable, always-on workloads, a 1-year reserved-instance or savings-plan commitment typically saves 30–60 percent over on-demand and requires no architectural change. Spot capacity is much cheaper but can be reclaimed, so it does not fit steady-state production. On-demand is the most expensive baseline. Dedicated hosts solve licensing and isolation needs and are more expensive than equivalent shared capacity.

questions.question: A team must guarantee that read-only audit logs in object storage cannot be altered or deleted by anyone — including administrators — for seven years. Which control most directly satisfies the requirement?
options: Server-side encryption with provider-managed keys
Versioning enabled on the bucket
Object Lock in compliance mode with a seven-year retention period
Lifecycle rule that transitions objects to a cold-storage tier after 30 days
questions.explanation: Object Lock in compliance (WORM) mode enforces an immutable retention period that even the root account cannot shorten or remove, which is exactly what regulatory retention requires. Versioning alone keeps history but lets privileged users delete versions. Encryption protects confidentiality, not immutability. Lifecycle tiering changes the cost class without preventing deletion.

questions.question: After a recent deployment, a microservice's latency P95 has tripled but error rates and CPU are normal. The team uses distributed tracing. Where should they look first?
options: Inspect the trace spans for the slowest dependency call — typically a downstream database, cache, or third-party API
Restart every pod in the cluster until the issue resolves
Disable distributed tracing because it adds overhead
Roll the whole region over to a disaster-recovery site
questions.explanation: Distributed tracing exists precisely to attribute latency to the span responsible — a slow downstream call (DB, cache, external API) is the typical culprit when CPU and error rates look healthy. Rolling pods is a guess that destroys evidence. Disabling tracing removes the very tool that points at the cause. A regional failover is a heavy, customer-impacting response that should never be a first step for a latency-only regression.

questions.question: A regulator requires that cardholder data and analytics workloads run on segregated networks with controlled egress. Which design best satisfies this requirement in a cloud environment?
options: Place all workloads in a single flat VPC and rely on host firewalls
Use separate VPCs (or subscriptions/projects) per trust zone, connected through a hub with explicit egress controls and inspection
Tag resources with a 'PCI' label and let billing alarms enforce segregation
Run everything serverless so no network controls are needed
questions.explanation: A hub-and-spoke design with separate VPCs (or subscriptions/projects) per trust zone and centralised egress inspection enforces network segmentation at the cloud-network layer, which is what regulators such as PCI DSS expect. A flat network with only host firewalls collapses the blast radius and trust boundary. Tagging is a metadata convention, not an enforced control. Serverless workloads still ride over networks that must be controlled.
